noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to predict the electronic configuration of atoms of the elements from hydrogen to krypton inclusive and their ions, using s, p, d notation and electron-in- boxes notation
understand that electronic configuration determines the chemical properties of an element

primer.text: An atom's electron arrangement is its chemical destiny. This note orders sub-shells by energy with the 4s-before-3d exception, writes configurations in full, shorthand, ionic and box forms, explains chromium and copper's anomalies, and converts configuration - groups, periods, blocks, full sub-shells - into chemical behaviour.

lessons.title: Filling order and block structure
lessons.opening: Electrons queue by energy: shells rise with n, sub-shells order s-p-d-f, and 4s queues ahead of 3d. This lesson turns that order into a prediction engine and maps the Periodic Table's four blocks.
keyPoints: Principal shells rise in energy with n; sub-shells order s, p, d, f within a shell.
The 4s orbital fills before 3d, the one standard exception to numeric order.
All orbitals in a sub-shell are degenerate - px, py and pz share one energy.
The Periodic Table's blocks are named for the sub-shell holding each element's outermost electron.

low.restatement: Fill 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, then 4s BEFORE 3d - the queue is by energy, not by number.
low.analogy: It is a canteen queue: the 4s window opens before the 3d window despite its smaller number.
low.examPointer: Krypton (Z = 36) is the ceiling for prediction at this level.

medium.restatement: Energy, not arithmetic, orders the queue: 4s sits slightly below 3d, so potassium and calcium end there; from gallium onward the written configuration lists 3d before 4s in numerical order.
medium.analogy: Bookshelves stacked by weight, not by label: the heavier 3d books wait on the lower shelf even though their index number is smaller.
medium.examPointer: Degeneracy of px, py, pz justifies Hund's rule drawings in the box notation.

check.stem: Which orbital fills first, 4s or 3d?

options.text: 4s, because it sits slightly lower in energy than 3d
options.explanation: Energy, not index, sets the queue.
Numeric order misleads here - this is the classic exception.
Filling is sequential.
Capacity never sets the order.

check.stem: An element has its outermost electron in a p orbital. Which block does it occupy?

options.explanation: Blocks are named for the outermost electron's sub-shell.
That requires an outermost s electron.
That requires a d-orbital outermost electron.
That requires an f-orbital outermost electron.

check.stem: What does degenerate mean for the px, py and pz orbitals?

options.text: They share exactly the same energy within the sub-shell
options.explanation: Degeneracy is equal energy, which is why they fill singly first.
They do share shape, but that is not the term's meaning.
Degenerate means equal energy.
They point along different axes.

check.stem: Potassium (Z = 19) queues nineteen electrons. Which full configuration results?

options.explanation: Eighteen electrons fill to argon; the nineteenth enters 4s, not 3d.
The 4s-first rule overrides.
That breaks argon's 3p6 completion.
That is calcium's count (20).

check.stem: For elements from gallium onward with electrons in 3d, how is the FULL configuration conventionally written?

options.explanation: Once 3d is occupied, the written form lists sub-shells numerically.
That is the FILLING order; writing follows numbers.
The d electrons are always listed.
The written convention switches once 3d holds electrons.

check.stem: State the energy order in which sub-shells fill from 1s through 4s.
State the four Periodic Table blocks and the criterion that assigns an element to one.
check.modelAnswer: The s block, p block, d block and f block - named for the sub-shell holding the element's outermost electron.

check.stem: Explain why the 4s-before-3d exception is described as energy-based rather than numeric.
check.modelAnswer: The filling order tracks orbital energies: 3d's energy rises slightly above 4s once the third shell fills, so electrons settle into 4s first; if numbers governed the queue, 3d would precede 4s, but the observed configurations of potassium and calcium prove energy rules.

check.stem: Predict the full configuration of an element with 19 electrons and name the block it occupies.
check.modelAnswer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1: the outermost electron sits in an s orbital, so the element (potassium) belongs to the s block.

lessons.title: Presenting configurations and their exceptions
lessons.opening: Configurations come in full and shorthand dressings, ions adjust the outermost electrons, chromium and copper break the pattern, and box notation draws the spins. This lesson covers all four presentations plus the transition-metal electron exit rule.
keyPoints: Shorthand notation brackets the nearest preceding noble gas: [Ar] 4s1 for potassium.
Negative ions add electrons to the outer sub-shell; positive ions remove them from it.
Transition metals fill 4s first but LOSE from 4s first when ionising.
Chromium ([Ar] 3d5 4s1) and copper ([Ar] 3d10 4s1) trade one 4s electron for a stabilised half- or full 3d sub-shell.

low.restatement: Write everything out for the full form; swap the noble-gas core for its symbol in the shorthand; ions adjust the ends; boxes draw the spins.
low.analogy: Full form is the complete address; shorthand is 'the Argon building, room 4s1'.
low.examPointer: Ca2+ ends as [Ar] - identical to argon's configuration.

medium.restatement: Ionisation order matters because 4s, though filled first, sits farthest out once 3d is occupied: cations strip 4s before 3d, which is why Fe2+ is [Ar] 3d6 4s0, not 3d4 4s2.
medium.analogy: The 4s electrons moved into the house first but live nearest the front door - when guests must leave, they exit first.
medium.examPointer: Titanium's box notation keeps both 4s electrons because 3d is neither half-full nor full - no promotion occurs.

check.stem: What is potassium's shorthand configuration?

options.explanation: Argon accounts for 18 of the 19 electrons.
Neon accounts for only 10 electrons.
Krypton comes AFTER potassium.
The nineteenth electron enters 4s.

check.stem: Calcium's shorthand configuration is which?

options.explanation: Two electrons beyond argon fill 4s.
4s fills before 3d.
That is potassium's count.
Neon's core misses eight electrons.

check.stem: When calcium forms Ca2+, which electrons leave?

options.text: The two 4s electrons, giving a configuration identical to argon
options.explanation: Outer-shell electrons leave first.
3p lies below 4s in the outer shell.
Ionisation strips the outer sub-shell pair.
Core electrons never leave in ordinary chemistry.

check.stem: Why is chromium's configuration [Ar] 3d5 4s1 and not [Ar] 3d4 4s2?

options.text: A half-filled 3d5 sub-shell is energetically stable, so one 4s electron promotes
options.explanation: The exchange stability of half-full 3d wins.
It can; the promotion is energetic, not a capacity issue.
It does; the promotion still applies to the 24th... which chromium lacks - the point is the 5-1 split of its 5 valence electrons.
Filling order still runs 4s first.

check.stem: Transition metals fill 4s before 3d but ionise 4s first. Why?

options.text: Once 3d is occupied, the 4s electrons are the outermost and easiest to remove
options.explanation: Filling order and removal order differ.
Mass is irrelevant.
They are removed at higher ionisations.
It is an experimental fact.

check.stem: State the shorthand configuration of calcium and of the Ca2+ ion.
check.modelAnswer: Calcium: [Ar] 4s2. Ca2+: [Ar] - after losing both 4s electrons the ion is identical to argon, matching it exactly.

check.stem: State the anomalous configurations of chromium and copper.
check.modelAnswer: Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1 (not 3d4 4s2) and Cu is [Ar] 3d10 4s1 (not 3d9 4s2) - both stabilise a half- or fully-filled 3d sub-shell.

check.stem: Explain why writing the full configuration of gallium places 3d10 before 4s2 even though 4s filled first.
check.modelAnswer: The full configuration lists sub-shells in numerical order for readability once 3d is occupied: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p1; the filling ORDER (4s first) describes how electrons arrived, not how the address is written.

check.stem: Write the full configuration of the Ca2+ ion and state which neutral atom shares it.
check.modelAnswer: Ca2+ is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 - exactly argon's configuration, identical to the noble gas, since both 4s electrons departed.

lessons.title: Configuration decides chemistry
lessons.opening: The electron arrangement is destiny: groups share outer-electron counts, periods share shell counts, and noble gases' full sub-shells explain their aloofness. This lesson converts configuration into chemical prediction.
keyPoints: Elements in the same group share the same number of outer electrons.
Elements in the same period share the same number of occupied shells.
Full sub-shells plus high ionisation energies make noble gases chemically inert.
Configuration therefore predicts how an element is likely to react.

low.restatement: Read the outer electrons off the configuration: that count predicts the bonding behaviour.
low.analogy: The outer shell is a shop's display window - what reactions see and trade with.
low.examPointer: Helium, neon and argon all end in full sub-shells - quote that trio when explaining inertness.

medium.restatement: Chemistry is electron exchange, so identical outer-electron counts give identical valency patterns down a group, while shell count fixes the period; the stability of complete sub-shells shows up as high ionisation energies and reluctance to react.
medium.analogy: Groups are families with the same handshake; periods are generations wearing the same number of coats.
medium.examPointer: Relate reactivity to configuration explicitly - it is the 2.15 discriminator.

check.stem: What do all elements in the same group share?

options.text: The same number of outer-shell electrons
options.explanation: Group membership IS outer electron count.
That defines the period.
That would make them identical elements.
Mass varies across any group.

check.stem: Why do helium, neon and argon rarely react?

options.text: Their electronic structures hold full sub-shells, and their high ionisation energies confirm the stability
options.explanation: Complete shells leave no easy electron to trade.
None of the three is.

options.text: Because they are monatomic gases with low mass
options.explanation: Mass and state do not decide reactivity.
They hold full complement.

check.stem: An element's configuration ends 3s2 3p5. What does the configuration predict?

options.text: Seven outer electrons - group 7 behaviour, one electron short of a full p sub-shell
options.explanation: The outer count is 2 + 5 = 7.
The group follows the TOTAL outer count, not the last sub-shell alone.
The p sub-shell is one short of full.
No incomplete d sub-shell exists here.

check.stem: How does electronic configuration explain periodic trends in properties?

options.text: Properties are a function of atomic number, whose configuration consequences repeat group by group and period by period
options.explanation: The repeating outer-shell pattern drives the repeating properties.
Masses rise continuously.
Density is not configuration-driven.
They follow directly from configuration.

check.stem: Using configuration, which pair shares chemical similarity most strongly?

options.text: Sodium and potassium, both ending in s1
options.explanation: One outer s electron each - same group handshake.
s1 vs s2 differ.
Full shell vs lone s1.
Full shell vs lone s1.

check.stem: State what members of the same period share.
check.modelAnswer: The same number of occupied shells - the same principal quantum number for their outer electrons.

check.stem: State the two configuration features that make noble gases stable.
check.modelAnswer: Full sub-shells in their electronic structures and correspondingly high ionisation energies.

check.stem: Explain why knowing an element's block helps predict its chemistry.
check.modelAnswer: The block names the sub-shell receiving the outermost electron, which fixes how many electrons the element typically gives, takes or shares: s-block elements lose one or two, p-block elements complete their p set, so the block is a one-glance reactivity summary.

check.stem: Helium, neon and argon share full sub-shells. Use their configurations to explain why they appear at the end of each period.
check.modelAnswer: Each closes its period with a complete sub-shell set - He ends 1s2, Ne ends 2p6, Ar ends 3p6 - so nothing further fits at that energy level and the next element must open a new shell, marking the period boundary.

glossary.definition: The statement of how an atom's electrons occupy shells, sub-shells and orbitals, in full or shorthand form.
Configuration written with the nearest preceding noble gas in brackets, as [Ar] 4s1 for potassium.
Box notation drawing each orbital as a box with arrows denoting electron spins.
Sharing exactly the same energy, as the three p orbitals of one shell do.
